transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I… I came in because I keep having these thoughts that maybe it’d be better if I just didn’t wake up. Like, I’m tired, but it’s not just tired from work—though installing carpet, tile, all that, it wears your body down, and crews notice when you’re not pulling your weight, you know?

And sometimes I think… dying would be the fair punishment for what I’ve done to my family and my crew. I know that sounds awful. I keep going over it in my head, like I messed everything up and maybe that’s what I deserve.
Have you ever acted on these thoughts or done anything to try to harm yourself?

I… I don’t know if I’d say I’ve done something, like an actual thing. It’s more that I keep thinking it’d be better if I just didn’t wake up. And then my mind goes to this place where dying feels like… like it would be the fair punishment for what I’ve done to my family and my crew.

I know you asked if I acted on it—I’m trying to answer. I just get stuck on the thought, like when you’re laying flooring and one piece is off and then the whole room looks wrong, and you keep seeing it no matter what. That’s how it feels in my head.
Have you had any specific plans or thoughts about how you might end your life?

I don’t… I don’t really have, like, a clear plan I’ve written out or anything. It’s more the thought that I shouldn’t wake up. Like I go to bed and think maybe that would be easier, maybe that would be what I deserve.

And then I start thinking about my family, and the guys on the crew, and all the ways I’ve let people down. It’s like when you’re cutting tile and one bad cut ruins the whole line, and you can’t stop seeing it. I just keep thinking dying would be the fair punishment for what I’ve done.
How long have you been feeling this way, with these thoughts about yourself and your future? Has it been going on for weeks, months, or longer?

It’s been… longer than weeks. I think about a year and two months now. It started a few months after my husband got hurt.

At first I thought I was just stressed, you know, because when someone gets injured everything changes—schedules, money, the house, who’s doing what. And I kept telling myself I just needed to push through, like on a job when the floor underneath is uneven and you think you can still make it work if you just keep going. But it didn’t really go away. It just kind of stayed with me.
Have you noticed that you don’t take pleasure in things you used to enjoy, or that you’ve lost interest in activities that mattered to you before?

Yeah… yeah, I have. I used to paint, like not anything fancy, just little things, and I liked cooking big meals—too much food, my husband would say, like I was feeding a whole job site. And I used to run before work sometimes, before a flooring job, just to get my body moving.

And theater rehearsals too… I used to actually care about showing up for those. Now it all feels like chores from somebody else’s life. Like I look at the paints or think about cooking and it’s just… why bother. If I miss rehearsal, I don’t even really care the way I should. It’s like those parts of me got packed away somewhere and I don’t know where I put the box.
Do you feel down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, not just during certain moments or when you're thinking about specific things?

I don’t know how to measure “most of the day,” exactly. I mean… I feel low a lot, but it’s not like I’m watching a clock and marking it down.

Some days it’s just there in the background, like dust from grout that gets into everything, even after you think you cleaned it. But then I’ll get distracted by work stuff or some stupid errand, and I don’t know if that counts as not depressed or just… busy. I’m not sure I can answer it cleanly.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual, or maybe feeling restless and unable to sit still, like you're physically slowed down or sped up?

Yeah… I think so. It’s not exactly like I’m just walking slow, though sometimes I do feel stuck.

At work I’ve caught myself pacing the same hallway with my trowel in my hand, going back and checking the grout lines again and again, like I missed something obvious. And then other times I’ll just freeze in a doorway. Like my feet won’t go, because it feels like if I move, something bad is going to happen.

It’s embarrassing because there’s work to do, and people don’t want to hear about you standing there with a tool in your hand like you forgot what doors are for. But yeah… restless and stuck, both, I guess.
Do you often feel like you’re a failure or that you’ve let people down in a way that makes you feel worthless?

Yeah. I… I do. It’s hard not to.

I keep thinking maybe I’m the reason everything around me goes bad. Like my husband got worse because of me, because I didn’t do the right things or I made the house feel… heavy, I don’t know. And then with the crew, when jobs got messed up or we lost work, I’d go over every little thing I did, like if I touched it, I ruined it.

Clients’ homes too—tile, flooring, whatever—people trust you to leave it better than you found it. And I keep feeling like I poisoned everything I put my hands on. Like I don’t just make mistakes, I make things worse by being there.

Sorry, that sounds dramatic. I know it sounds dramatic. But yeah… I feel worthless a lot. Like whatever happens to me, I probably earned it somehow.
Have you found yourself feeling guilty about things that you normally wouldn’t, or feeling like you’re to blame for things that weren’t really your fault?

Yeah… guilty, definitely. I blame myself for things that, I guess, if someone else said it, I’d tell them they were being unfair.

But in my head it lines up. Like my husband getting worse—part of me keeps thinking I caused it somehow, or I didn’t stop it right, or I made everything heavier. And then with the crew losing work, or jobs going sideways, I’d go back through every little thing I did, like maybe I was the bad luck in the room.

Even clients’ houses… if something got messed up, I’d feel like I ruined it just by being there. Like I poisoned what I touched. I know that sounds… extreme. But it feels true a lot of the time. Like whatever happens to me, I probably deserve it.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight over the past year—like eating a lot more or a lot less than usual?

Yeah… I think it’s less. Most days I don’t really eat until late, and by then it’s like I remember I’m supposed to, not because I want to.

Sometimes I’ll make something or pick something up and then take a few bites and my stomach just turns, like I can’t get it down. It’s annoying because when you’re doing floors or tile you’re supposed to have energy, you know, and everyone’s always got gas station food or someone’s sandwich sitting in the truck, and I just… forget, or I look at it and feel sick.

My work pants have been getting loose too. I’m not trying to lose weight. I actually hate that, because then I notice it when I’m kneeling or my belt doesn’t sit right, and it makes me think about it more. So yeah, my appetite’s definitely been off.
Do you feel like you're worthless or excessively guilty nearly every day, or does it come and go depending on what’s happening in your day?

It’s… it’s most days. I don’t want to say every second, because sometimes I’m busy measuring or cutting or trying to get through a job and I’m just focused on not messing up the next piece, but it’s kind of sitting there underneath.

Like I’ll be doing something normal and then it comes back—my husband getting worse, the crew losing work, a client’s house getting messed up—and I think, yeah, that’s me. I’m the common thing in all of it. Like I brought something bad into it, like I poisoned everything I touched.

And then I start thinking whatever happens to me is probably fair, because I must have earned it somehow. So… yeah, it comes up nearly every day. Even when nothing big happens that day.
Have you noticed any trouble thinking clearly, concentrating, or making decisions, even with simple things?

Yeah… I do. It’s like my brain just… gives out.

Like I’ll carry one box of tile, just one, and by the time I set it down my whole body feels like wet cement. Then if I have to answer a couple client messages—nothing complicated, just “what time are you coming” or “which grout color”—I’ll stare at the phone like it’s written in another language.

And then I can’t decide simple stuff. Like whether to load the cutter first or the buckets, or which message to answer, or if I should stop for food—well, not food, just… you know, normal little choices. I’ll stand there too long and people think I’m ignoring them or being difficult, but I’m just stuck. My head gets so tired it’s like there’s no room left to pick anything.
Have you noticed that you have significantly less energy than before, or that even small tasks feel exhausting to you?

Yeah… a lot less energy. It’s like I don’t have any reserve anymore.

Like I’ll carry one box of tile—not even a big run, just one box—and by the time I put it down my body feels like wet cement. And then if my phone goes off and it’s just a couple client messages, simple stuff, I’ll be staring at it like… why is this so hard?

It makes everything take longer. I’ll stand there trying to figure out what to do next, like load the buckets or answer the message or move the cutter, and my head gets so tired I can’t even make the simple decision. It’s embarrassing, because people probably think I’m lazy or dragging my feet, but I’m just… wiped out from almost nothing.

inference_history.note: Initial presentation includes recurrent thoughts of death and self-punishment, suggesting severe depressive symptoms. Possible major depressive disorder, recurrent depressive disorder, or prolonged grief disorder.

The patient's symptoms have persisted for over a year, beginning after a significant stressor (husband's injury), and include persistent guilt, anhedonia, and suicidal ideation without a specific plan. This supports major depressive disorder (F32.2) and rules out adjustment disorder (F43.22). Recurrent episodes cannot be confirmed without history, so F33.2 remains a candidate but less likely at this point.

The patient's symptoms have persisted for over a year, with no indication of improvement or remission. The severity of the depressive symptoms—including persistent low mood, guilt, anhedonia, psychomotor disturbances, impaired concentration, and suicidal ideation without a specific plan—suggests a diagnosis of moderate to severe depressive episode. Given the duration and severity, and lack of indication of manic or hypomanic episodes, the diagnosis is shifting from moderate (F32.2/F33.2) to severe (F32.3/F33.3).
